utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have appearances for Defence counsel who are all present this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present on behalf of the Trial Chamber, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel for the accused, and everyone else in this courtroom. We'll be hearing a witness scheduled for today, but before we do so, we have to deal with the documents that are to be tendered into evidence. There's one outstanding question in relation to these documents. It concerns the expert report which was provided to us in the English version. Does Defence Counsel have a B/C/S version of this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we apologise. We did not include a B/C/S version of the expert report with the other documents, but since the witness did draft the report in his own language, we will now provide the B/C/S version to the Registry, the B/C/S version of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, any comments to make with regard to the B/C/S version of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber will have a look at the B/C/S version of the document. Mr. Registrar, could we have definitive exhibit numbers for the documents that are being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll start with the first documents that were dealt with at the hearing two days ago. The first one will be DH1601, and the English version exists which will be DH1601/E. DH350 is admitted into evidence. The English version will be DH350/E. DH351 is admitted into evidence. The English version will be DH351/E. DH362; the English version will be DH362/E. DH354; the English version DH354/E. DH356; the English version will be DH356/E. DH353; the English version will be DH353/E. DH1598; the English version will be DH1598/E. DH1590; the English version will be 1590/E. DH378; the English version will be DH378/E. DH358; we only have an English version, so the number will be DH358/E [as interpreted]. DH510; the English version will be DH510/E. DH1599; the English version will be 1599/E. DH1398; the English version will be DH1398/E. DH104 admitted into evidence; the English version will be DH104/E. DH1623; the English version will be DH1623/E. DH1624; the English version will be DH1624/E. DH1625; the English version will be DH1625/E. DH1626; the English version will be DH1626/E. And finally, 1627; the English version will be DH1627/E. As far as the following annexes are concerned, DH357 will be admitted into evidence, and the English version will be DH357/E. DH358; the English version will be DH358/E. DH359; the English version will be DH359/E. DH363; the English version will be DH363/E. DH1589; the English version will be DH1589/E. We will now deal with the expert report. It will be DH344, and the English version will have the number DH344/E. And finally, there were a series of maps, 17 in total. The number will be 345 for the entire series of maps, and each map will also be marked with numbers 1 to 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, when looking at the transcript, I get the impression that Exhibit 350 is missing. I can't see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If I omitted it, I apologise. DH350 is admitted into evidence, and the English version will be DH350/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If anyone notices any omissions, we'll have time to put this right. Turning to the Defence now, we have three witnesses scheduled for the next two days. Could the Defence proceed in a manner that will enable us to hear these three witnesses over the two-day period. We don't want to have to make the third witness stay during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we had a one-day break because we were not able to bring a witness here on that day for the reasons that I have already mentioned, Defence counsel, when preparing for the examination of this witness, tried to limit itself to the most essential events so that although we intended to examine the first witness for two hours, we will try to keep this to an hour and a half at the most. And this should make it possible for all three witnesses to be heard this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll call the witness into the courtroom immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you're receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say that you can hear me and that you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I'd be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sejad Jusic. I was born on the 16th of April 1968 in Jezerci Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you employed at the moment? What is your professional status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a policeman in the Travnik police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what position did you hold or what duties did you perform at the time? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a policeman at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that occurred in your country in 1992 and 1993? Or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have OTP investigators interviewed you or have you never been interviewed as a witness for the purposes of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think anyone from the OTP has interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel who will be examining you, I would like to provide you with some information. This is what I do whenever a witness comes to testify. I do this in order to put the witness at ease, but also to inform the witness of the procedure that will be followed. You have just taken a solemn declaration, and you have said that you will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. As you are aware, this implies that it is your duty not to lie. As a policeman, you know that false testimony is an offence. Secondly, when answering questions, you should be aware of the fact that whatever you say cannot be used in a subsequent prosecution against you. So you may feel quite free to answer all the questions. I should also inform you that you will have to answer questions that will be put you both by Defence counsel. They have told me that they should be examining you for about an hour and a half. After that stage, you will have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution who are to your right. As a rule, their cross-examination should take as long as the examination of the Defence, about an hour and a half. The three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time if they feel it's necessary to clarify some of your answers, or if they notice that there are some gaps in your testimony and it's important for the Judges to fill them in. In such a case, we will ask you questions. Once we have asked you questions, the parties have the right to ask you additional questions in relation to the answers you provided to the Judges' questions. If you feel that a question is too complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. The questions put to you must be clear to you, and the answers you provide us must also be clear because you should be aware of the fact that we don't have any written records. This is an oral procedure. As a policeman, you know what this means. So it is your oral testimony that is important. And if necessary, your oral testimony will also be supported by documents shown to you by the Prosecution or the Defence. But at this point in time, we don't have any written documents that concern the testimony you will be giving us. And this is why your oral testimony is so important. If you encounter any difficulties, inform us of the fact. We're here to resolve any problems that may arise. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. The hearing will take a certain amount of time, and it might be tiring for you, but rest assured we will be having a number of breaks. Every hour and a half, we have half an hour break. This should allow you to rest, and we have these breaks for technical reasons, too. The breaks are not intended to enable the Judges to rest. Without wasting any more time, I will give the floor to Defence counsel now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the important information that the president of the Trial Chamber has provided you with, I would also like to ask you to wait a little before answering the questions that I put to you. Since we speak the same language, it is necessary for my question to be interpreted so that the Trial Chamber and everyone else in the courtroom can understood the questions I put to you. So before answering my questions, could you please pause briefly. Have you understood what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, where do you live at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I live in Jezerci in Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live at the beginning of the war in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was also living in Jezerci at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber that you were a policeman. Could you tell us a little about your educational background. Which schools have you completed, when, and where did you complete them?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I completed secondary school in Travnik. And in 1991, I finished a course for policemen in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which duties did you perform and for how long did you perform these duties up until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As a policeman -- as a trainee, I started in Donji Vakuf, which is near Travnik. That's where I was when the war broke out. At that point I moved to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you serve in the army? And if so, which army did you serve in and were you conferred a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA, and I didn't have a rank of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, since you have already said that in the course of 1992 and 1993 you were a policeman, where did you work as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Donji Vakuf to Travnik, I worked there briefly. And then because it was impossible to go from Jezerci to work in Travnik, they moved me to a police station, a police outpost in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, as a policeman working in the Mehurici police outpost, were you a member of the civilian or of the military police force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the civilian police. The M-U-P, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, who was your superior? Who was your boss, or rather, what was the chain of command within the civilian police? What sort of hierarchy existed there?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The Travnik police station had its own chief and its own commander. In fact, the public security station. I made a slight error. The public security station had to report to the CSB, the Security Services Centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can speak a little faster. You just need to pause when you have finished your answer.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Very well. So they were subordinated to the CSB in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any time in the course of the war did the BH Army -- was the BH Army in charge of the entire civilian police force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No. Sometimes part of the police force were subordinated to the army, but I'm not aware of this being the case for the entire police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was your police outpost, or rather did some members from your police outpost at any time in 1992 or 1993, were they at any time subordinated to some BH Army unit? And if that was the case, could you tell us when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, for about 40 or 45 days, we were subordinated, but I can't remember the month. I think it was towards the end of the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of those 40 or 45 days in the summer of 1993, where did the police return to? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they returned to their usual duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the main task of the civilian police at that time? And before?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, protecting public order, crime prevention, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the civilian police, which organ was responsible for preparing criminal reports for the competent judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the crime police who worked in Travnik. In Mehurici we didn't have such a force, but we provided them with the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police outpost in Mehurici, how many professional policemen did this outpost have in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was the only professional policeman, and I started working in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, apart from yourself in the police station, were there any other policemen? If so, were these active-duty policemen or were they reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They were all from the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many men did you have in the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I think we had about 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jusic, if you can remember: What sort of educational background did the people who were called to the reserve police force have? And had they obtained at any earlier date any kind of experience in police work?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I knew most of them. They were neighbours of mine. They weren't very educated, and I don't think that they had ever been trained as policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, why didn't you call people who had professional experience as a policeman to the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't decide about such things, but at the time there were no such men in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, in the area you performed your duties, were there any BH Army formations?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did those formations also have formations involved in policing? In other words, did they have a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military police presence in that area covered by the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of relationship there was in 1993 between you and members of the military police. Were there any issues on which you sought to work together?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: There were jobs that we did jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your personal skills and knowledge and the jobs that you performed together, can you estimate whether the military policemen of the army possessed the necessary professional skills for the duties they had to perform at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't believe they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, what area was covered by your police outpost?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The area around Mehurici, which includes several villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How simple was it to control that area; and if there were any problems, why did they exist?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Mehurici police outpost did not have any vehicles. The villages were rather scattered over the territory. The roads were bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did those features of the terrain and the level of your own equipment influence your ability to perform your duties?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They did, as did the general condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you a question that you might be able to answer as a policeman. Before the war, during the war, and generally speaking, what agencies deal with the presence and movement of foreigners in a country?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian police always had a body in charge of foreign nationals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In which particular body of the police did such agencies work?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that something like that existed within the CSB, the centre of security services.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you in your police station have any duty to monitor, record, or report to your superior authorities any presence or movement of foreign nationals in your area?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We did. We noticed that some foreign nationals were appearing, and we wrote that in our reports to the police station in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already told me about the manpower of your police station. Tell me now about the level of your equipment. What kind of weapons did the civilian police dispose of in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Most of us had rifles; that is, long barrels, as we call them. But none were issued by the service, so if you wanted to have one, you had to bring it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that everybody who had to be mobilised into the police had to bring their own rifle. Where did people get rifles?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I suppose they bought them on the black market.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Responding to my previous question, you said you had noticed some foreign nationals in your area, that you had drawn up appropriate official notes that you forwarded to the public security station in Travnik. Tell me, when did you notice those foreigners and who were they?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: It was, I believe, in late 1992. They were from Arabic countries, judging by their appearance and clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said "judging by their appearance." What does that mean? What kind of clothes did they wear?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They wore some kind of short slacks or trousers and some capes that I used to see on television. Or cloaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from a secondary school, and after that went through a police training course. Tell me, did you know anything before the war about the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in the community where you lived, were there stories circulating? Was there any information about those people, who they were, where they were located? Did your community in Travnik have any knowledge about those people?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, since up to the elections of 1990, the prevailing system in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not look kindly upon nationalistic tendencies or aspirations. Do you know anything about the views of the then authorities about expressions of nationalism, nationalistic opinions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a crime. It was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did that attitude change in any way after the 1990 elections? And if it did, how did it change, if you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a change. Some parties were established then that displayed nationalist tendencies and even outbursts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice such outbursts? Did they come to your attention? And do you remember how they affected your immediate environment?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I remember, for instance, the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, you lived in Jezerci, and you worked in Mehurici. And you noticed some foreigners there from Afro-Asian countries. Do you know why they were coming to your area, and did you give any thought at all to the reasons that could make your area interesting to those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't give it any particular thought then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In late 1992 when you became aware of their presence, did you know where they lived, where they were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I know for a while they were in the school building in Mehurici. Later, when some sort of detachment of the BH Army was formed, they were chased out of there. In any case, they were no longer in that schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jusic, where did they go from there?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They went to a place called Poljanice, to the family estate of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Safic family where they set up some sort of camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you as a policeman became aware that this camp was guarded in some way, or was access to the camp free?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The camp was guarded, and as far as I know, access was prohibited to everyone but their own members, not even the police could enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent were you able to gather information about those foreigners? Did you know their number, their origin, things like that?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At the outset when they had just begun arriving, we tried to inspect the identity papers of some of them. We couldn't speak to them because of the language barrier. They would tell us their names, but we were not able to see their papers. And as far as we were able to understand, they had none. Later, they were constantly moving around. You see them today; you don't see them any more tomorrow. It was very difficult to track their movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a policeman, did you notice that in a certain way there was a rapprochement between them and the local population, or did they stay closed in their own camp? Did they keep to themselves?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: In a way, there was a rapprochement with them and the local population because they donated money and some packages to people. They also provided some young men with arms and took them to their quarters. They got married, some of them, to local girls, and thus established bonds with the local families.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was their influence, especially among the refugees and the other local population? Did some people view them with sympathy, others as cause for concern? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: There were people who were against their presence. But let me tell you, there were many refugees there who didn't have homes in their area. And these people helped them. Somebody who receives money and food and help from you is bound to have some sympathy for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice how those men were armed? In other words, what kind of weapons did they give to those who joined them?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They were well armed. They had a large number of vehicles. And whoever joined them also received weapons. And moreover, all of those who joined them had their families taken care of as well by those men. Such families received a monthly allowance, assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your job of maintaining public law and order, or rather in the course of performing your duties, did you become aware of any incidents involving or caused by these men, these foreigners, and did you try to investigate such incidents?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: There was a number of such situations. There were a number of catering establishments where alcohol was served. They would enter such establishments and break everything. Furthermore, problems occurred when they would come across a girl who was not dressed according to their code or their idea of propriety. But they didn't want to discuss it with us. We noted this in certain official notes. They would go back to their camp, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you attempt to enter the camp, investigate those persons, and elucidate what really happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, policemen, have the possibility to use force and attack that camp in order to enforce the law and perform your basic duties by use of force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, it wasn't possible. They outnumbered us, and they were better equipped, better armed. At that time, you tried to avoid conflict and incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that you didn't have enough manpower -- could you please repeat your answer to the previous question because the interpreters didn't hear all of it. Please speak up if you can. You said it was not possible for you to attack them. They were better armed, better equipped, and you were trying generally to avoid conflict. What else did you say?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We had previous police reports about policemen who had already been wounded or hurt in such incidents, and our commanders insisted that we should avoid such conflicts and keep our people safe. It was from the relay in Vlasic that we received such reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the overall situation and the sympathy a certain part of the local population had toward -- with them, would a decision to enter into a conflict with these men or attack them be something that a local police station could take? Or would it require superior authority?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We couldn't do anything on our own. That's certain. That had to be resolved at some higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about a different subject, Mr. Jusic. In the area where your police station was active -- in fact, in this entire area from Travnik to Zenica, were there other police stations and where were they located?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: There was a police station in Han Bila, another in Mosor, and I don't know exactly the date but I believe there was a police station at Ovnak. That was a separate police station that had been established by our former Croat colleagues who had previously worked together with us. But I don't know the exact date when this separate police station was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice in 1992-1993 that in addition to army units, some other military units were present in the area; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: There were units of the HOS, the Croatian armed forces, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a time when you became aware of a certain conduct by certain military units that affected the personal safety of people and the public law and order in your area?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Situations were frequent when somebody would go to Travnik or Zenica only to be stopped by men who were told to wear insignia of the HVO or HOS, and the person who would report the incident would say that these military men would take away their money and valuables and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jusic, which roads were available at all to go to Travnik, Zenica, or Vitez from the Biljanska Dolina, Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Those were roads through Maline and Guca Gora up -- in Guca Gora, there was the HVO road. From Bila to Travnik and Vitez, there was also an HVO checkpoint. And towards Zenica, the road held two checkpoints, both of the HVO and the Croatian civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 19, line 3, it says "men who said." What it should say is "men who wore." I would like this corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel did not quite understand what is actually written in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me continue: You said there were checkpoints on those roads held by the HVO or the Croatian civilian police. Tell me, did you personally as a policeman have such experience in connection with this mistreatment of people or people being stopped at checkpoints held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but once as a policeman on duty I went out in the field to intervene somewhere, and I was stopped in Cukle by some Croats. I don't know to which exact unit they belonged. They stopped me, together with four or five of my men, also Muslims. I was wearing a police uniform, and I had heard about an incident in a village overlooking Cukle. So I went out to investigate. I was stopped and detained for four or five hours. I was disarmed. My sidearm, my pistol, and the rifle were taken away from me and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the civilian police or the army, if you know, made any attempts to iron out such clashes, and what was the reaction of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the HVO after such attempts?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I know that from the Travnik -- from the public security station, our commanders insisted that there must be no conflict between Muslims and Croats in that area. We had to report everything to them rather than allow ourselves to be involved in an incident of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me question you now, Mr. Jusic, about your knowledge of certain specific events. Where were you on the 24th of April 1993? Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I do. I was in Mehurici. On that day, I don't remember whether I was on duty or I was off duty in Mehurici, but at one point I noticed that those men, those mujahedin led through Mehurici some people from Miletici, both Muslim and Croat by ethnicity, and took them away in the direction of the Poljanice camp. And most of us who were standing there had no idea what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was there a time when you realised that the army command located there was seeking to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: You mean the problem that occurred in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that some Bosniak Muslims and Croats were taken away from Miletici. Did you realise that the command of the battalion that was based there was trying to find a way to free these people, or you were not involved in that at all?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was not involved at all, but I knew the command was in the schoolhouse that was close by, and I realised that they were all agog.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out that these people had been released from Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did find out about that, but I don't know the dates. I know that after a certain period of time, they were taken away by UNPROFOR to Novo Bila, I think, and there were some sort of joint HVO and army commission that went to that site. I think the civilian police was involved as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time take over a task that related to the remaining population in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I remember that afterwards, an old woman and her husband remained in Miletici. I can't remember her name now. Our task was to visit that family every day on a number of occasions to see whether there were any problems, to speak to them, and this is what we did. I think the man's name was Zdravko, and I don't know what his wife's name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The policemen who visited that family and were concerned with their security, did they ever tell you about the attitude of their Muslim neighbours in relation to those people who had remained in the village?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I myself often visited that family up there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to point out to the interpreters that we are not receiving any interpretation. Please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You started answering my question. You said that "I often visited that family myself." You didn't finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I visited the family. I would sit with them, speak with them. They said that their neighbours from Miletici, Muslims, would come, ask them about what they ate, how they lived. And they said that the Muslims would bring them food.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jusic, could you please tell me where you were on the 8th of June and how long had you been where you were on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, I was at home in Jezerci. I don't know the exact dates, but the situation was such that -- well, first I'd have to tell you about the villages and how they were mixed Muslim-Croat villages. The situation was such that it was not possible to go out of the village for a few days. There were -- there was fire that had been opened on our village. It wasn't safe to go out. So I think that I stayed at home for two or three days. I wasn't able to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was attacking your village? Or rather, who was attacking that road that you used to get to work?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say where the shooting was coming from, but I think it was from the place called Balte. I think that that's where they were firing from. It's the road above the village of Zelce [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in the village of Jezerci, did you notice that the BH Army at the time, before the 8th of June, was itself launching attacks against HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the army wasn't present in the village of Jezerci at the time. There were some old people with old hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, when you were in the village and during the period that you weren't able to go to work, as you said, could you find out that there were any attacks on other Muslim villages in the Bila Valley? Could you please speak up because the interpreters can't hear you, and it makes it difficult for them to do their work. Tell me, did you find out about any attacks on villages where the Muslim population was in the majority in the Bila Valley? If so, could you tell me which villages were attacked and when.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I heard about the place called Ricice. Then there was Velika Bukovica. I also heard that Velika Bukovica was attacked, and that some people, some women were taken away to Busovaca. I heard that people from Cukle were not able to move around. They couldn't leave their village. And before the 8th, a few shells fell on my village, on Jezerci. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you have a Motorola or some sort of communications equipment that you could use to obtain such information?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, no. But at night, someone would come to the village and inform us. An army member would come home to have a bath and then provide us with information. That's how I found out about such things. At the time, there was no electricity in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, on the 8th of June 1993, you were also in Jezerci.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you go to work in the village of Mehurici for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, a day or two later. I don't know when exactly. Our commander at the time, he was the commander of the station. He'd been cut off. He was in Travnik. He couldn't go there. And a day or two later, we met, the policemen met in Mehurici. We set off to work again until someone came from Travnik and appointed me as a commander up there in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, a few days after these events you were appointed as commander of that police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went there two or three days later, what did you find out? Did you notice that any people had been brought to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we found out that there were quite a lot of civilians in the Mehurici primary school. They were in the sports gym. They were of -- and there were some military-able men there. And the army told us that we should guard these men. Our task was to guard these men to make sure that nothing happened. The people kept in the school were of Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take over the task that your superiors from Travnik assigned you?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you then find out why these civilians had been taken to Mehurici and placed in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: This is my opinion, and this is what I heard from army members. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond They were there in the school for security reasons. Apparently, there were mujahedin who were moving around the villages, and they could have done something to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues have just pointed out that in English and French -- my question was "brought to Mehurici and placed in the primary school." In French, it says "imprisoned in the primary school." So I just wanted to point out that there was a difference in translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who took care -- who was concerned with the accommodation of the people in the primary school and who was responsible for their food?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why were these people placed in the gym in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no better place for them at the time. There was no better accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, was there a motel of some sort or a hotel in the village of Mehurici? Or some other facility that could have been used to provide a certain number of people, two or three hundred people, with accommodation? That's the number of people who had been placed in the primary school.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the gym was the largest place. There wasn't a hotel at the time. That in my opinion was the only place available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, tell me, how many policemen were involved in providing them with security?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, taking care of them was our priority. We weren't really involved in any other duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While performing those duties, while taking care of the safety of the people in the primary school, did you hear about anyone being treated inappropriately? Did you hear about anyone being maltreated? And if so, did you take any measures?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The women, children, and old people were placed in the school. If they wanted to go out, they could go out and light up a cigarette. Equipment, money, all their valuables, these are items they kept with them. At the time, there wasn't much of a selection, but it was possible for one of us to go and buy something for them. But no one told me about any kind of maltreatment or any kind of problems in the school. There was someone called (redacted), and if any of them needed something, they would address her, and what could be done would be done. We all ate the same food.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since a minute ago you said that the mujahedin were in Savici Kuca in the Poljanice village, could you tell me whether your policemen ever informed you about some mujahedin trying to enter the gym; and if so, what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion, I don't know whether there was just one mujahedin or a number of them, they wanted to enter the gym. The policemen didn't let them enter. Weapons were drawn, but they didn't get in. I don't know what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, were you informed about a soldier behaving in an inappropriate way? And if so, do you know what measures were taken against such a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember such a thing. I remember that the brother of one of the soldiers died in the conflict with the Croats, and there was one prisoner whom we would take to be bandaged every day, and one soldier hit him while he was being taken away to be bandaged. But as far as I can remember, I think that the commander imprisoned him for 15 days. I can't remember exactly. But I know that the military police took him away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up. The interpreter can barely hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have the word "prisoner" here, could you tell us whether this was a person in a gym or were these HVO members who were in the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about military-able men in other rooms. A wounded HVO soldier would go to be bandaged every day. I don't know his exact name. On that occasion, an army member hit him when he was on his way to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the military police took him away, and that he was punished. This has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether you were aware of the fact that during that 15-day period while they were there, were you aware of the fact that any representatives of humanitarian organisations came, members of the Red Cross or European Union observers? Did any such people appear there?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I know that Red Cross representatives came, and I think that European observers also came. They didn't have any particular objections to make. They saw what the situation was like. They realised that we couldn't do anything better.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that they kept their personal possessions. What sort of possessions did these civilians have, and the HVO members who were detained in another area?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: When the civilian police started taking care of them in order to prevent anything happening to them, they had some money, some bags on them at the time. No one touched that. As for the military-able men, they didn't really have many possessions, but they had money that they had in their pockets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When they left, did they leave with all these possessions, all these things?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, please tell me, while they were there until the time they left with UNHCR or with someone else, I don't know with whom, during that entire period, what was the situation like in the Bila Valley? Was there any combat going on or had peace been fully established by that time?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was combat action going on at the time, not really in the vicinity of Mehurici, but a little further away in the direction of Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the police force in such conditions were you able to take those people to their village and guarantee their safety?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, no, we weren't really secure at the time. So this is not something we could have guaranteed for these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened to the people for whom you were providing security? Can you tell us where they went?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The civilians were exchanged. I don't know after how many days exactly. And the military-able men, when it was possible to safely take them to Zenica, to the penal and correctional facility, the KP Dom, they were all taken there. But it was risky to take them via Ovnak. But as soon as we had the opportunity to take them to Zenica without risking anything, they were taken there to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is mumbling and it's difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you ever find out that some of the men -- please, could you tell us whether you were ever informed that some of the men who were taken from Maline to Mehurici were taken away somewhere, and did you find out if that were the case who took them away?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, later, when the people were going to Mehurici under military police escort, it came to light that the mujahedin had singled out some people up in Poljanice, and no one knew where they were after the mujahedin had separated them. That's what people would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the duties you had, the duties that you have already mentioned, did you compile an official record, and did you inform your officers, your superiors in Travnik about this event?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we did make a record. This information hadn't been verified, but a record was made and forwarded as far as I can remember. It's possible that the mujahedin took some people out of the column, and nothing was known about the people after this had been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this event, were you able to go to the mujahedin camp after this event in order to obtain additional information about what had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No. We were not able to enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question I have already put to you, you said that at some time in the summer, you were resubordinated to the BH Army. To which brigade were you resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was resubordinated to the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you resubordinated before or after your Croatian neighbours had left for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: This happened afterwards, after the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you have these combat assignments?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: For about 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, since you have told us that your duties involved attempting to provide security for people and preserve public order, tell me: Did you notice property being looted from abandoned Croat houses? And if so, did you take any measures?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Houses abandoned by Croatian neighbours were frequently looted. Some of them were torched. Some people set fire to them. We dealt with these cases. But it was difficult at the time to discover who the perpetrators were because first of all there were a lot of refugees in our area. These were people whom we did not know. The troops were also present. And if we found any items and confiscated them, we didn't know to whom these items belonged. So a lot of items that the Mehurici police station confiscated couldn't be returned. There was no one to return to them. So these items were on the whole lost. But we were engaged for about 45 days. We didn't do -- we didn't perform any other duties. We were at the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, you said that even when you found property that had been looted, you weren't able to establish the identity of the perpetrators. Why not?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if some of my policemen were near such houses and knew who the owner was, then we would know who the injured party was. But frequently, we did not know who the owner was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you kept those items in the police administration in warehouses of some kind. Tell me, why didn't you return that property to the owners of the houses when you knew who the owners were? And could you protect such houses from being looted again?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We kept these items in the police station, but if we had returned them to the houses, someone would have probably taken them again because the area was a large area, and it was not possible for the police to control the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 31, line 18, it was interpreted as my question whether it was possible to identify the perpetrators. And my question was actually whether it was possible to identify those who suffered damage or loss. And the witness answered appropriately. So I would like this to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, since in this area where you guarded those things -- you had this area where you kept things in safekeeping. Did it happen in 1993 that some of the injured parties actually came looking for their things, wanted them back?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No. In 1993, we did not have any such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, in Mehurici or around that area, did you have a possibility of finding a safe house, a storage place where these items could be kept safe from damage, safe from wear and tear, weather, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We only had two rooms for the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jusic. Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have concluded your examination-in-chief in good time, as you said you would. It's half past 10.00. We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution so they can conduct their cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone and to Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and I'm a representative of the Prosecution in this matter. As indicated by the President of the Trial Chamber, I'm going to ask you a few questions. However, if you feel at any point in time you have not understood the question or you want me to repeat something, please feel free to interrupt me and I will try to oblige.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we could indicate on the record that the Defence for Mr. Kubura has no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to ask the other Defence team whether they had any questions to put to the witness. I apologise. I forgot to put this question to you. But you are at some distance from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Benjamin, thank you for the remark you made. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, you outlined for the Trial Chamber your role as commander of the Mehurici police force at the time, and your duties. Now, could you state clearly for us when you actually took up the duty as commander of the police station in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was after the outbreak of the conflict between the Muslims or the BH Army on the one hand and the Croats on the other hand. A couple of days after the outbreak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that previous to that, which would be probably around the 10th of June or thereabouts, previous to that you worked as an ordinary policeman in an outpost in Mehurici? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, your role as an ordinary policeman in the outpost in Mehurici and when you became a commander, your role and your duties remained basically the same. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Correct, with the proviso that I conveyed to the other policemen the orders I was receiving from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, could the witness be shown Exhibit P204, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. P204.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The document basically outlines -- it has to do with your resubordination to the 306th Brigade. But correct me if I'm wrong, it basically outlines the duties and the functions of the MUP. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I received my orders from the police administration in Travnik, and they must have agreed this prior to that on a higher level. They must have previously agreed this should be like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I'm in total agreement with you, because you see, it clearly says -- it identifies the duties quite clearly. It says that you are to -- for instance, number 3, secure vacated settlements by daily patrols, prevent torching and looting, and use mobile checkpoints to control minor roads, secure captured persons. And number 7 in particular, individual movement by armed persons must be stopped, and these persons disarmed and registered. Did you see that forming part of your duty, to protect public order and in crime prevention? Did you see that as part of your duty, number 7 in particular?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin. Witness, this document the Prosecution is showing to you, and I can see that it was addressed to the MUP in Mehurici because under number 7, it says MUP Mehurici. Were you yourself familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend, you indicated that there came a time when you saw the arrival of foreigners into the area of Mehurici. Now, am I correct? Because you'll have to answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber give us an estimate of the population of Mehurici in the period we're talking about, January 1993 to 1994 or thereabouts. Could you give us an idea of what the population of Mehurici was like.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Around 10.000, I believe more than 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to tell us around how many of these foreigners you would have noticed at that time in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At what time precisely? In 1993? 1994? Or earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I speak of when you started seeing them, when they began emerging. And if they increased, could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They didn't arrive all at once. They arrived gradually. At the beginning, there was one or two, then more, until their number eventually increased. But it was the police who was supposed to establish their number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I am aware that the police were supposed to establish their number. And which police do you mean when you say "the police were supposed to establish their number"?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I meant the civilian police. I meant the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Weren't you a part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So it's by virtue of your being a part of the MUP and later on being a commander of the Mehurici police station where basically the great numbers of the foreigners were seen. It's in that context that I ask the question. Could you give us an idea, an estimate of how many of these people were in the area. Let's put it late 1992 ending up in 1994. How many people, would you say?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you the number. How shall I put it? All of them looked the same to me. I couldn't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You knew for a fact -- and you indicated to us that there were about 10.000 inhabitants of Mehurici. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, around that. But you see, there was a lot of movement of the population, refugees coming and going. The number was never constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I can understand. So this is my question now: Do you think that if there were 10.000 foreigners, you would have been able to assess if there were 10.000? Would you say that there were 10.000?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, no, there were not that many. There were less.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That's just a point. Would you say that there were a thousand?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So at least we have some kind of figure to work with. We have a thousand foreigners who emerged into Mehurici according to you, approximately a thousand. And we have a population of approximately 10.000, plus or minus, you know, due to the movement. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there were not even a thousand. But okay. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I don't think that we would expect you to know the exact number, but we just want to have an idea of whether there were the same amount of the population, if they were in the minority or if they were in the majority. Were they in the minority?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They were in the minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How would you describe the situation in Mehurici, let's say, from about January 1993 onwards, until mid-1994? How would you describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: What is exactly the object of your interest here?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, I have to ask the questions. I ask the questions; you provide the answers. And my question to you is how would you describe the situation in January 1993 and onwards, to about mid-March 1994, in Mehurici? That's all.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as Mehurici and the surroundings are concerned, including a couple of villages around Mehurici, there were both Muslims and Croats. There was a majority of Muslims. This mujahedin camp was set up in the place called Poljanice. And we, as the police, carried out our duties, our regular duties under the new conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But I don't think you understood the question. Were the relations in Mehurici between the different ethnic groups great, wonderful? Was it a tense situation? How was that period then in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As for the relations between the Muslims and Croats in that area, I have already mentioned in my testimony that checkpoints had been established. Mehurici was divided from Travnik and Zenica, and we always used roads to leave Mehurici, and we would always come across checkpoints set up by the Croatian side. Our people would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. If you had to use one word to describe the situation, what would that word be?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Difficult, tricky. I don't know which word. Tricky.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would I be correct if I had said to you or can I put to you that the situation could be described as tense?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And would I be correct in saying, then, that the emergence of these foreigners was part and parcel of the tense situation that existed in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: That also had an impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Their presence then fuelled the fire. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you as commander of the MUP, the civilian police, and your role being to protect and serve basically and prevention of crime and protecting your civilians regardless of ethnic background, how did you see your role with respect to the foreigners who came in?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, when they just started arriving, we tried to inspect their identity papers. We couldn't find a common language. We couldn't speak to them. We had no interpreters. They didn't seem to have any identity papers. And at the beginning, they settled in the Mehurici schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But as a police officer and as a commander, you have certain powers. Am I correct? Powers of arrest being one of them. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could you tell me why you refrained from arresting or dealing with these foreigners who were in the minority that came into Mehurici and who, according to you, appeared to be causing a lot of chaos? Why you personally, as a commander, and why your force didn't do anything to stop what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would appreciate it if my learned friend would perhaps specify the period for the sake of the witness. Does her question refer to the period when he was a regular policeman or later? Because the period she set up initially is rather broad, 18 months or so. The question doesn't sound very clear to us. I don't know if the witness is able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, I think I established from the very beginning that the witness was a police officer in the first instance, and then he became a commander. So during the period, 18-month period, he was a police officer, albeit a junior, and then he became the commander. So it's in his capacity in both roles, as a police officer, his duty as an ordinary police officer, and his duty when he became commander. And I think he's prepared to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've heard the question. Please answer the question, which is a very precise one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when they just began arriving, they didn't cause any problems when they were small in number. They would come by night, settle in the schoolhouse. They would go to the mosque. They would have some limited contacts with those segments of the population who were more religious than others. But there were no problems with them. So that we didn't have any need to arrest them at that time, but we did inform our force at the base in Travnik that they were starting to appear, and we were told to try to find out who they were and where they were coming from, to see their papers. And that proved to be difficult. They didn't have any papers or they didn't show any to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So we would go back to the part of the problems -- we've finished with the part when they weren't giving problems. We will move on to the part when they started being problematic. Before I go on to that, could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us who gave these people permission to settle in the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was not accountable for the school. I was not responsible for it. We had our base in the police quarters. And I don't know how they ended up in the schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you happen to know, then, how they got through the HVO checkpoints? How did they get through? How did they get to you in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they managed to do that. But there were cases when they were found dead. One of them was found dead, killed in a place called Zukica Bridge. How they passed through, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could I suggest to you then, Mr. Jusic, that they may have been a part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, you as a civilian police, who is supposed to protect and serve and who is supposed to uphold the law, allow a bunch of foreigners, and from your explanation, they refused to show their papers - most likely they didn't have any, so they were probably illegal as well - you as a commander never thought it prudent that you should sort them out, do something about them? Didn't you think it would have been the prudent thing to do?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I informed headquarters in Travnik, but I myself wasn't in a position to take any action in the area. In my opinion, this is something that should have been dealt with at a higher level, if I or the civilian police in Mehurici were to take any action.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And so I believe that you will agree with me, then, when I -- after looking at all the possible ways, you would agree with me that I say that they had to be a part of this army? They had to have some kind of nexus with somebody; hence, the authority that they presented. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question is asked and answered. The witness has already answered this question in very precise terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, you've asked him the question again. He said he didn't know. So there's no need to ask him the same question again since he has told us that he couldn't say whether they were part of the army or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, this could be considered to be harassing the witness, which is not your objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that's not my intention, Mr. President. Mr. President, may the witness be shown P775, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to paragraph 2, and in particular, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague has now distributed a document with the possibility of asking questions in relation to this document. Well, questions can only be asked if one establishes that the witness has already seen this document or was familiar with it in some other way. If no grounds have been established for asking the witness questions about this document, it shouldn't be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, on the 20th of June 1993, were you resubordinated to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. But I don't know whether that was the date. I do remember that we were resubordinated for a 45-day period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the 20th of June 1993 would have been included in the 45-day period. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has again said that he was resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. However, this document, as far as I can say [as interpreted], is from the 7th Muslim Brigade, and I do not see what relation it has to the answers the witness has provided so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the Prosecution -- let the Prosecution finish their questions because there is an obvious link, because Document P204 dated the 18th of June resubordinates them to the 306th. And we have a document dated the 20th of June 1993 which comes from the military authority, and a reference in this document is made to a detachment and to the MUP. He himself was a member of the MUP, and therefore he could perhaps tell us why this document dated the 20th of June mentions MUP since on the 18th of June the Mehurici MUP was resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. Ms. Benjamin, ask the witness the question that relates to line 9, or rather that relates to the paragraph you were referring to. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I originally indicated to you line 9, but because of my friend's objection, I'll just take you up to one, two, three -- the third line of paragraph 2 so that we can establish the foundation. And it speaks about "along with 15 MUP members under the command of the command of the 2nd Detachment..." So does this document say to you that the MUP was involved in this situation? Does it say so?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before. The area it referred to -- the area of Bijelo Bucje is not an area in the vicinity of Mehurici. Within the Travnik MUP, there were other police outposts, but this does not concern or is not related to the outpost at which I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm very well aware of that. But I just wanted -- for her to see that the MUP was involved in this, because you're part and parcel of the MUP, aren't you -- weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
