utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just said that he had nothing to do with this or with this area. The witness isn't familiar with the document. If he was never present in that area, and the Travnik area is a vast area, how can my learned colleague continue to ask this witness questions? We can all see that it says MUP in this document, but this has nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, the witness has said that this document does not concern him because of the resubordination of the MUP in the Bijelo Bucje area, but this was not his sector. But you have come to the conclusion that MUP may have been related to the 7th Brigade. But not to this witness, in any event. That's what the Defence has pointed out, and quite rightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, and I could not agree more. But the point that the document is being used for is really for line 9. I drew his attention to line 3, too, so that my learned friend would realise that the MUP, MUP all over, wherever, were subordinated to the 306th in different areas. And the question is not in respect to the battalion that was in that particular area, and if she allows me to ask the question, she'll see where I'm coming from. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel, with regard to the 306th Brigade in this document, unless I'm mistaken, I don't see that the 306th Brigade is mentioned. 312th Brigade has been mentioned, the 7th Brigade, but I can't see a reference to the 306th Brigade in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I indicated before, the document is not produced for the brigade that the witness is subordinated to. The document is produced to show what went before it with respect to line 9, and it was the same question that my learned friend accused me of asking the witness twice. So I was just about to use the document to draw his attention to find out whether my conclusion was correct with respect to line 9 and the foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But in line 9, line 9 of which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Of paragraph 2, Mr. President. Earlier on I had asked the witness if he believed, in light of all that had transpired, if he thought or he agreed with me that the mujahedins, because of all their power or apparent power, could have been aligned to the army, ABiH army. And he said no. And I want to draw his attention to line 9, to get his opinion on what is there. That has nothing to do with who he's subordinated to or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll translate line 9 now. It says that in the course of the action for soldiers, foreigners, Arab foreigners, were killed, as well as three other soldiers from the 312th Brigade. That's what line 9 says. And you want to ask him whether he was aware of the fact that four foreign soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In duty along and aside with the 312th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But he was not a member of the 312th. How can he answer the question if he wasn't a member of the 312th? He was a member of the 306th. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. For two or three times, you have tried to explain to my learned colleague that this is not a witness who could provide a witness [as interpreted] to such a question. And secondly, that the document itself demonstrates that it refers to some other order, not an order about which my colleague asked a question. We have brought two members of the 312th Brigade here, and if my colleague had wanted to discuss this matter, she had the opportunity to do so. This witness cannot provide any additional information in response to the question put to him by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, you have heard what I have said; you have heard what Defence counsel has said. This member was not a member of the 312th Brigade, and therefore he cannot answer questions about an operation that concerned the 312th Brigade, since he was only resubordinated to the 306th for a number of days. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution will rest on that issue. With all due respect, Mr. President, could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P430, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, you had earlier indicated to us that around the date of this document, which is the 24th of June 1993, you were commander in the police station in Mehurici, and you were resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. I'm correct, am I not?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date on which we were resubordinated. But if you referred to some event, that might help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, if you can recall the document P204 that was initially shown to you and you said you recognised, that was dated the 18th of June. And that was the document that was talking about the resubordination. And the 24th of June is after the 18th of June. So you would have been resubordinated then. Thank you. I would like you to look at paragraph 2 in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, my learned colleague asked a question, and I didn't hear the witness answer the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I indicated to you that based on Prosecution Exhibit 204, which was dated 18th June 1993, with respect to the resubordination, that P430 was dated the 24th of June 1993. So definitely you would have been resubordinated by then?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, we don't have to be probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you show him the document, P204, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That's the first document we showed you. If you look at the very top of the document, it says "18th June 1993." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if you look at number one under "Order." Okay. And if you look at P430, and the date is?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the 24th comes after 18, so you were already resubordinated. Am I correct? Okay, now we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 2. Have you gotten to the end of paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you -- in light of -- in light of an answer that you gave to my learned friend in respect to you yourself visited the Mehurici school and that your duty was to protect the civilians there, in light of paragraph 2, could you explain to us exactly what has transpired there? Because something seems to be amiss. So could you clarify it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian police provided security for the civilians in the school and for HVO prisoners who were kept in two garages. I don't know how else to describe them. No one reported any incidents of maltreatment of the civilians or of the soldiers. I remember one event, one or two mujahedin wanted to enter the sports hall in which the civilians were kept. But the police prevented them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would it be correct then, and correct me if I'm wrong, to say that the civilians at the Mehurici school were properly treated? Or would it be incorrect to say that?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Given the conditions or the facilities we could provide at the time, well, they ate the same food that I ate, and it wasn't possible for us to provide them with better conditions. I think we provided them with the best possible conditions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But surely, these are very strong words. "They are subject to lethal danger." Could you tell us who -- or rather, do you know what was referred to as the "death brigade"?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Why would you think that the members of the commission for prisoners would be concerned about the 247 civilians of Croatian nationality in the gym? Why do you think that they would be concerned if, in fact, as you say, the civilians were properly treated? Why would you think that they would express concern?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they were concerned. But as far as I'm concerned, and my men, I know that the civilians were treated correctly. Even today, I meet people who were there. Even today, I meet such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that the Mehurici school was guarded by the military police? Am I correct? Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps from the beginning, but we the civilian policemen took over. But we did cooperate with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if I say to you that these foreigners that you told us about who came into Mehurici, if I say to you that they were also guarding the school, would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us when they were guarding the school.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I only know that they were in the school at the beginning, and then they went up to the camp in Poljanice. But I'm aware of an incident. I remember an Arab coming. He wanted to enter the gym where the civilians were kept. But the policeman prevented him from doing so. I think that some MPs appeared rapidly as well, and this foreigner didn't enter the school. He didn't enter the gym. A record of the event was made and forwarded to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that this was your area of responsibility, so to speak, I take it that when you say to us that the foreigners and the mujahedins as they were later referred to as, had absolutely nothing in the control of the Mehurici school. I take it that that is what happened at that time. Okay. In your response to my learned friend, you said that the Red Cross had no particular -- could you respond, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you acknowledge what I just suggested, that in your area of responsibility as commander of the Mehurici police station, you are aware that the mujahedins were not in control of the school or not in any part responsible for the guarding of the civilians at the school?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, in answer to my learned friend, you indicated that the Red Cross had no objections with respect to the way the civilians were treated. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I said that I wasn't aware of them having any objections. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P740, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In particular, from line --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before my colleague moves on to line 12 or 13, as she said, it would again be necessary to establish the grounds on which she wants to ask this witness questions about this document. The witness should be asked whether he is familiar with the document. He should be asked whose document this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect to my friend, Mr. President, for the witness to compare a statement with another, he does not necessarily have to know the document or to whose document. The question will follow exactly what preceded. He said that the Red Cross as far as he knew raised no objections. This is a document by the Red Cross, and clearly -- I take it I can go ahead. I don't have to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's a problem as far as the dates are concerned. This document is dated the 4th of November, and there is a reference in the document -- to which period exactly? Which period is concerned by the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: It's dated 4th November 1993, and I think it speaks of -- it talks about in our letter of 16th October 1993. So it's around that period. And if my learned friend would realise that when I started off, I particularly asked the witness the expanse of the time that he held his role for, and he started off saying he was a junior police at the beginning and then he became the commander, and subordinated to the MUP thereafter for 45 days. So it's all during his tenure as commander. And I wanted to verify if this was the person that they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But -- Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't see any relation between this witness's testimony and the document referred to. All the questions put by my learned colleague concern the civilians who were in the primary school until the 24th of June. This document does not refer to that event or to the manner in which those civilians were treated. Secondly, the witness said that the Red Cross did not raise any objections when they visited the school. As you can see, this document is dated in November, and it comes from the HVO Red Cross. We have to see to whom it was forwarded. We don't see that it was forwarded to the witness. If the witness is to answer any questions, a relation has to be established between this witness and this witness's testimony and the document that the -- my colleague wants to show. I don't see such a relation, and I don't think questions can be asked relating to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The problem is as follows, as far as I can see: The witness says that he was resubordinated to the 306th Brigade for 40 days. If he was resubordinated at the beginning of June, in October and November he was no longer resubordinated to the 306th. The indictment concerns civilians detained in the Mehurici primary school up until the 24th of June. So the period referred to in this document does not relate to count 3 in the indictment. So we don't know, unless you have asked him the question, whether the people in the school -- but I'll ask him the question, and this will resolve the difficulty. Witness, as far as you can remember, in October -- of course it can be difficult to remember dates. In October or November, as far as you can remember, were there any civilians who may have been protected or guarded in the Mehurici primary school? As far as you can remember, was this the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there weren't any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you know, these civilians were protected until when, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the exchange. Until they were exchanged. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this exchange was about what time, July, August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe a month after they were brought from Bila. Maybe a month elapsed until the exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after the exchange, were there again civilians settled in the schoolhouse, or was it finished with the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was no one there any more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Prosecution, it seems to me difficult to find a link between the witness and what he says and the contents of this document concerning the alleged persons detained in Mehurici. That would be in October-November supposedly. The witness says there was no one. That's a different theory. But according to your theory, in October-November in Mehurici, could there have been sites of detention or detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Maybe if there was somebody in the mujahedin camp. That's the only thing I can think of, if any. As for other places, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer is that if there are any detained persons, it would be in the mujahedin camp, not in the schoolhouse. Very well. Ms. Benjamin, in these circumstances, we seem to be wasting our time with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. And I think I'll get it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, just verify for me the period of your tenure as commander of the civilian police force in the Mehurici area. When did you cease being the commander in the Mehurici area?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there long. A couple of months, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We know that you started in June. "A couple of months" meaning what?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was appointed commander there provisionally until they were able to send somebody with more experience. And when traffic on the road was re-established, a commander from Travnik, a new commander from Travnik arrived. So I was commander for about two or three months. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it that after you relinquished your portfolio as commander, you knew nothing that transpired in the Mehurici area.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I continued to work at the police outpost as a policeman, or rather deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you continued to work as a policeman, or rather deputy after you gave up the post of commander. And for how long did you practice as the deputy?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Maybe until 199 -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Until 1990.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm trying -- I'm trying here --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I help you. Was it to the end of 1993? Did you continue as deputy commander until March 1994 in the Mehurici area? Up to when were you -- the end of the year, the beginning of the next year?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was constantly there at the police station. I worked until 1995, 1996. I don't know how much it matters whether I was deputy commander or assistant commander. I can't be precise on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is my question to you: As deputy commander during that period, November 1993, would you have known whether there were detainees in the school in Mehurici? It was your area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has already answered this question. He said there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, it would be more purposeful to ask him something like this: You became deputy commander in June. Who was commander then? Because you were deputy. You must know the name of the person who was sent to work as commander during the months of September, October, November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe his name was Ahmet Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. At least this way, we made some progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Maybe you can help with this: Do you know of the blacksmith shop in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what transpired at the blacksmith shop in Mehurici during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any detainees housed at the blacksmith shop in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I know. There were members of the HVO detained there. I don't know how many, but I know they were located in two rooms. Everybody calls it blacksmith's, but those are actually two garages facing each other, not far from the police premises, the premises of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So the blacksmith shop, according to you, was close to the civilian police premises. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that's where you worked from. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As a member of the police force upholding law and order, didn't you think that you should have gone over to the blacksmith shop to investigate what might have been happening there?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We had the responsibility to watch over the detainees, the prisoners of war, so that they would be safe from harm by others. And I know only people from the military security organs were authorised to come in and take somebody away, perhaps. But I don't think anybody actually came. There was only questioning wherein they gave statements to security officers. Otherwise, they were guarded by members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 660, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this document is shown to the witness, I believe there is slight inclarity in the way this last answer was interpreted. So maybe my learned friend can go back to her previous question so that I don't retell the answer. Because I heard the witness saying that it was their job to take care of those prisoners and to take them to the schoolhouse where the security officer interviewed them. And it is formulated in the recorded answer in such a way that you don't see clearly who had what task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please rephrase the question so that we see exactly what was whose job.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I do not think that was what the question intended. But if my friend wants that answer, we can ask him outright.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us whose job it was to look after the detainees at the blacksmith shop.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: It was the job of the police outpost, the MUP outpost. My men, in other words. The civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did he get P660?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. There are two counsel on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would again ask for identification of the relationship of this witness with the document before any further questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You, too, have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have the same problem as before. This document is a military document dating back to the period when the witness who was working in the MUP was not resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. So it is our position that he should not be saying anything about it. He should not be commenting on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think somewhere in his testimony he spoke about the body of a foreigner who was found in Zukija Most Road. And I think it's very important for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution and the Defence for him to be able to clarify exactly what he was talking about. And my question to him would have been, if I would be allowed, in the second paragraph on page 2, was that the same person or is that the same incident that you had referred to earlier on in your testimony in chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can ask the question because there is indeed a link. He had really talked about foreigners who had been killed. So please go ahead, ask the question. Rephrase the question, please, because I don't think he understood it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, earlier on in your answers to my colleague, you indicated that there was a body that was found in Zukija Most Road. Do you recall? Yes. So my question is to you when you read the paragraph on page 2, is that what you were referring to when you responded to my colleague?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Can I first read this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1992, what I said about that foreigner, and an on-site investigation by the criminal investigation service was performed. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So this is 1993, so that's something completely different, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me see. I could not say if that is the same thing or not. It could have been in late 1992 or early 1993. But I already told you all I know about the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you will agree with me that -- or correct me if I'm wrong that some of these foreigners wore uniforms similar to those worn in the BH Army. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time all uniforms looked alike. And the foreigners wore some other kind of uniform. In fact, they wore something that looked more like their own traditional costume.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And my second-to-last question will be this, Do you -- rather, I wish to get your opinion on this: Do you as commander of the Mehurici police post and as a member of the police force who swears to uphold the law and to protect the citizens, do you feel in any way responsible for the chaos and the havoc that may have been wreaked by the foreigners who came into your country?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We experienced problems with the Croatian side even before the arrival of the foreigners, the mujahedin. As far as I can remember, I as a policeman was captured in the place called Cukle at a time when I believe there were no foreigners in the area. I also said, however, that the arrival of the foreigners only made things worse. But the problems existed even before, before I remember them being around Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I do not think you clearly understood what I was asking, so I'll ask it in this way: Do you feel in any way that you failed in your duty as commander of the police in Mehurici to the civilians of Mehurici? Do you feel that you failed in your duty in any way?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We had an outpost where we worked together, Muslims and Croats jointly. Then Croats left us. After that, we already had much less control over villages inhabited by Croats. I don't know to what extent I am guilty or responsible for that. It is up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you feel that in light of the fact, as you indicated to this Trial Chamber, that the mujahedins who came into the Mehurici area during your tenure and who, as you indicated, were in the minority, do you feel that the population, so to speak, was let down by the army, let down by the police? Do you feel this is how it is?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say to you that the mujahedins were allowed to do whatever they pleased during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I was not -- correction. They were not allowed, and they did indeed many things that we were not happy about, but we were unable to prevent it. The problem of the mujahedin should have been resolved at a much higher level than the level of my police outpost or police station. It should have been resolved at the level of the military police or higher up. At least, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And do you get the impression that there might have been a reason why this wasn't addressed?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the mujahedin did elicit the sympathy of some locals. Not all of them, but some. They married some young local girls. I don't know. I am saying about the mujahedin who were there. They helped people, but they also required people to abide by a certain dress code, cover their heads, et cetera. Some people who were more religious took them with more sympathy; others with less. It's very difficult to explain this situation. For instance, after they established these family ties with certain families, I would be arresting, for instance, the son-in-law of my neighbour who had married into that family, that mujahedin. You see?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And finally, my last question to you is would you agree with me if I say to you that the civilians were not in control of law and order, but in fact it was the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, maybe the witness understood the question of my learned friend, but I didn't because the question refers to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should specify this question which is, after all, rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: A while ago you indicated to me in response to an earlier question that it was difficult to deal with the mujahedins because of the connection they had with the locals, so to speak. So my question to you was who was in control of law and order? Was it the civilians or the police and the army? Who's in control of law and order?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The police and the military police. But I don't know how to explain to you the situation that prevailed then. There were front lines on both sides, and then you want some other problems on top of that. From the command of the MUP, we received instructions not to deepen the conflict, but on the contrary to try to smoothen things out. We were not looking for trouble. We were not trying to deepen the conflict. We did our job as best we could under the conditions of the war. It's not the same as peacetime. You should have been there and lived there for a while in order to understand. I don't know how to explain it to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusic. Mr. President, this ends the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have -- we will have about three-quarters of an hour after the break. There may be some additional questions, and the other Judges have told me that they also have questions for this witness. So as far as re-examination is concerned, how long will you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as the other Defence team is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we have any questions, it won't take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, that will take us up to 10 past 1.00, if the Defence needs 10 minutes. The Judges will have to ensure that their questions are concise so that we can finish by 1.45 because we have two other witnesses to deal with by the end of tomorrow. We will now adjourn, and we will resume at about 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to the Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jusic, as a policeman and as the commander of the police administration in 1993, what was your attitude towards the protection of civilians? Did you make distinctions of any kind which were based on their nationality or religion?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, my learned colleague showed you Document P204 dated the 18th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be shown to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, when answering a question put to you by my learned colleague, you said that an agreement had been reached at a higher level according to which you were to be resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. My learned colleague quoted some items from this order. At the bottom of the order, the addressees are mentioned. Could you tell me whether the obligations from 1 to 10 only concern you or all those who are mentioned in this document, all this who are listed in this document?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: It concerns everyone listed here at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question I put to you and to a question that was subsequently put to you by my learned colleague, you said that at a given point in time, you were engaged in combat operations for a 45-day period. Could you tell me where you were engaged in combat operations during that operation? Was that a combat line? Was that a defence line, combat position, or did that have to do with the tasks that are defined here?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: That had to do with the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to what extent did the new tasks you were assigned when you were resubordinated, and this task involved mounting a defence, to what extent did this influence your ability to carry out the tasks listed in this order?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: This had a great influence on our ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many policemen remained at the police station after you had left for the lines? How many policemen remained there in order to perform duties that related to public order, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Only two policemen remained there in order to cover that area and to make a note of any incidents, if there were any such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my learned colleague, you said that in order to understand the situation, it would be necessary to be in your position to see what was possible to do. Tell me, at the time, and in particular today, do you believe that using force against those individuals or foreigners, against those foreigners or individuals who were close to them, would using force have resulted in opening up a new combat front?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, given the conditions in Vlasic above us, there were Serbian positions there. On the other side, there were the Croatian positions. No one would have got involved in something like that. That would have been our end if we had started a conflict with the mujahedin. And later on, we settled accounts with them. But at that time, the conditions were different. And we believed that it was possible to deal with them. At the time, it was not possible to deal with them, and it would have been an error. We didn't have sufficient troops, sufficient forces to deal with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Jusic, is as follows: You gave a rough estimate of their number. You said there might have been a thousand of them up until the end of 1993. Tell me, why were they strong? Was it because of their numbers, their weapons, or were there any or factors that had to be taken into account consideration before taking energetic measures against them?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time there was information according to which in our area there were foreigners arriving from Herzegovina who also instilled fear. And when the mujahedin came, some Muslims accepted them, and they felt safer. But others didn't. And they had a little equipment, they had some money. So they went after young men, provided them with weapons. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If I have understood you correctly, would it be correct to say that you could not really assess what the consequences would be if other measures were taken against them? And my question is, although you have answered it, who -- whose responsibility was it to take measures in such conditions? Was it a military, political problem?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I think it was a political problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have only two questions that concern this very same document that the witness has before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you have a look at item 2 in this document, please, "Set up checking stations in the following places: "Lager, Ovnak, Han Bila, Gornje Puticevo, the entry and exit from Guca Gora." Was this order under item 2 carried out?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at number 3. Was this order carried out, the order regarding daily patrols and were other measures taken?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was hard to carry this order out. There were very few of us. Very few members of the civilian and military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now give the floor to the other Judges who have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did anyone ever report to you about crimes or offences as a policeman at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now. You mean while -- throughout the entire time I was in the police or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: I'm referring to 1993, to that period. Did you carry out any investigations into any crimes or offences?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At the time I was a policeman and later a commander. I had two years' experience in the police. I can't remember now if we had received any such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no one who would refer to you, who would report on crimes to you? The Prosecutor? Civilian authorities? You never carried out investigations of any kind? You never carried out investigations of any kind? You never carried out investigations into crimes?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, an injured party could report an incident to us. In such a case, it was our duty to take action and inform the authorities in Travnik, which is where the crime investigation police was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to the Mehurici primary school now. Were there any mujahedin who occupied the third floor of the school when Croats were detained in the school.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you can confirm that there were mujahedin there before the Croatian detainees arrived there in that school.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated in the school, but before that date, I don't know when, I think it was when a battalion in Mehurici was formed. I think that that's when they went to Poljanice and set up a camp there. But they weren't there before the Croatian detainees arrived in the school and were placed in the gym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For how long did you guard the school while Croatian detainees were held in that school.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we provided security for them right up until the exchange, for that entire period. But perhaps a day or two after the conflict, we didn't go into function immediately. The police had to gather, and then we took over the duty of guarding them and the soldiers who were in the garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you aware of what had happened in the school? Witnesses have appeared before us, and they have stated that there were prisoners, some Croatian prisoners who were beaten. Are you familiar with any such events.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. No one reported any such incidents to me. We had contact with a doctor. I can't remember her name. But if anyone in the school needed anything, she would take care of it. She would make requests for anyone who needed assistance. But she never contacted anyone because someone had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to another subject. You said that you were called when there was looting of Croatian houses, and you also said that you were not able to identify the looters. You weren't able to arrest anyone at all? You weren't able to arrest any of the perpetrators? No one was identified in the course of looting one of these houses.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, MUP did file criminal reports against certain individuals for having stolen Croatian property. Similarly, I remember that when the military police cooperated with us, then the commander would order that an individual found in the course of looting should be detained. But if we found someone who was transporting goods that we suspected had been obtained as a result of theft -- on the whole in such cases we didn't know whose property this was, we didn't know who the injured party was. We would confiscate these items, but most of these items were lost. We kept them, but the injured party never appeared to claim them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question. In response to a question put to you by Ms. Residovic, when she asked you why you weren't able to control the mujahedin when they maltreated the population, you said that you didn't want what had happened on Mount Vlasic to be repeated. Could you provide us with certain additional explanations, what actually happened on Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't quite precise. A lot of policemen were killed when defending the transmitter on Vlasic. I don't know if you're aware of this, but it happened in May of 1992. And what I wanted to say is we were ordered not to engage in a conflict with them so as to prevent our men from being killed. We were told to try and make compromises, and if not, to try and avoid making the situation even more tense. That's why I mentioned Vlasic, for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judge sitting to my left also has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, while I was listening to you some questions came up, and a number of them have been answered in the meantime. But some others remain. First, regarding your resubordination, I had a few questions that have been answered by you partially a few minutes ago. But just to check whether I have understood you well, when you were telling us about the investigations of looting and setting of fire of houses, that period on which you told us a number of things, that was not while you were resubordinated, was it? It was in a different period.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat my question then. You told us you were resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. And after the break, you said "I went to the front" in response to a question put by the Defence. In the beginning this morning, you told us that you were engaged while you were in Mehurici in preventing looting or investigating looting and preventing houses from being burned and confiscating goods that had been looted, all that activity. My question is that activity was not in the period you were resubordinated, but in a different period. Is that right? Is that a proper understanding of what you said.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: In a period of 45 days, only two men were left at the police station, and at that time nobody from the civilian police was able to deal with these incidents. They were only able to guard their own premises. We dealt with these investigations both when we were resubordinated and when we were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So while you were in the army, you had nevertheless time to investigate cases of looting and burning of houses, et cetera? Because now you said I did this during the subordination period and outside the resubordination period. So it's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: While we were resubordinated, in one period of this resubordination, the entire police unit was on the front line for 45 days. At that time, we didn't have time to deal with it. But the military police did deal with it. That's the only such period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you been resubordinated several times or not.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think that was the only time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm asking this because the document that has been shown to you, P204, suggests that you were resubordinated in order to investigate, together with others, cases of looting and torching, et cetera. But I'm not sure. So that's the reason why I ask you.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true. But during this particular stint of resubordination, I told you already, we were on the front line. There was a shortage of manpower. Only during that period. We couldn't investigate then because there were not enough people on the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me then ask you a few questions on the events in April in Miletici. You said that you were not directly involved in negotiations to release the prisoners taken by the mujahedin, that you afterwards got an order to go to Miletici to visit the old couple and to check whether they -- everything went well with them. Did you also talk to them, to this man and woman.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Every time we went up there, it was our duty to talk to them so that they can tell us if they had any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And did they tell you the story of their -- of what happened to them in April.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: For the most part, our discussion revolved about what their life there was like. They said that the Muslims from Miletici brought them food, and we wanted to know whether anybody was doing them any harm in that particular period, whether anybody was interfering with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did they speak about the events, for instance, who had been killed, or did they keep their silence about it.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: They were our neighbours. I don't know. We didn't talk about that. We didn't ask them, and they didn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you have other information enabling you to tell who had been killed in the situation.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We knew -- in fact, I was in Mehurici when the mujahedin passed through escorting the people from Miletici. So that's only what I saw. But I wasn't part of the investigation, and I wasn't there when the joint commission came. I just had that task to see them from time to time and talk to them. And if there was anything to report, I was to report it to the police station in Travnik, and even the military organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... situation on the events and send it to Travnik to the MUP or to the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: A official note was written summarising our knowledge of the affair, but we didn't go out into the field to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And that note was written by you or by the then commander or by whom.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you now, but I know for certain that it was written, and the report was sent on to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the information in the report, what was its basis? What were the sources of information being used in this report.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: What we were able to gather through operative work without going on the site, but otherwise the majority of the locals of Mehurici were there, and they could see those Muslims and Croats being led by the mujahedin towards the camp in Poljanice. And that is the information underlying the report that was sent to the base in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You wrote in this report or some other person was based on what the population told you as the police and what the army told you. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Regarding Maline, I have a few questions to put to you. 8

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge. Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On Maline, you said "I wrote a report and I sent it to Travnik." I have a few questions on that. Was it a long report? Was it a short report? Can you say anything about the length and content of the report?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Can you -- are you able to recall what your sources of information were regarding this report? Who gave you the information you put in your report.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Regarding Maline or regarding Miletici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Regarding Maline this time, yes. I'm now talking about Maline.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Analogously after this clash with the Croats, people were talking. It was common knowledge that mujahedin singled out some people from the column and took them away. Nobody knew where. They took them away in the direction of the Poljanice camp, and these Croats were not seen later. That's what we heard, but we had no more precise information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said it is -- it was common knowledge that mujahedin singled out some people. This is my next question. Who told you so? Were these eyewitnesses? Were these other people who had heard it from other people? How direct were your sources of information.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I heard that much later, long after the event. I don't know how long, but it could have been as long as a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And did you speak with eyewitnesses, people who had seen the events themselves, or with other people.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We didn't speak to eyewitnesses. It's a story that made the rounds among the people, so it reached me about a month after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it had some characteristics of a rumour, then? It's difficult to substantiate in your case. That is the situation.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Having written your report, you sent it to Travnik. And could you tell me to what authority in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: All reports should go from outposts through the commander to public security stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you also send a copy - I don't know whether this was practiced in your organisation, but did you also send a copy to the public prosecutor in Travnik? To a public prosecutor or judicial authority.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The police outpost was only in contact with the public security station. And our criminal investigation service was the one who had contacts with the judiciary and the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you ever get or ever notice a reaction on your report from the part of the competent authorities in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the outcome. I have never been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the same, I take it, is true for your report on Miletici in the month of April? You have never heard anything about steps being taken by the competent authorities in Travnik? Or have you.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No. But I know that a joint commission had gone out for an on-site inspection, a joint commission of the police and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were told that it was in the purview of the army. It was their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is, in fact, true. That we know also, yes. You said twice, I think, during this morning "it was not my duty and my" -- "these are not my possibilities to do criminal investigations myself. I was the only professional in the team in Mehurici, and we had no means to do these things." So you only reported suspicions to the competent authorities in Travnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, that's how things stood in that period regarding Miletici and Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm asking this because you could in theory think of other steps to take. You could, for instance, interview potential witnesses who were in the school in Mehurici. You could go to Maline itself and interview people there. You could go to the army and say "well, do you know about the case?" You already said it was impossible to interview mujahedin. But the other steps, were they also practically impossible for you to take.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, concerning the HVO soldiers detained there, and the civilians -- in fact, I'm not sure about the civilians. But as far as the military are concerned, interviews were conducted by the security organs of the brigade. Men from the military security organs. And we were only told to guard them and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you ever consider asking the army to help you to interview mujahedin who could have been involved in the events?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: No, I never asked the army to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And why didn't you do it?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we sometimes tried to speak to the mujahedin, but they refused to speak to us. But we cooperated with the army; that is to say, with the military police within the army. But not with the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did the military police or the army offer you any help -- offered you help in your investigations? Did they say, well, let's assist you in discovering what has happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian police didn't carry out any investigations into those events. Military security did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. That's in line with what you said before, yes. I have still one or two questions on the people locked up, or if I may say so, in the elementary school, people who were there for some time. Has any of them ever asked to you or to another civilian policeman to be released?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I know that they asked some of the policemen to bring them some photographs from the houses that they used to live in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And if any one of them would have asked that to you, "please let me go," would you have allowed that?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I would have reacted at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was it you who had the power to decide these matters? Or was there a higher-up authority?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't have the authority to make such decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So who was it then? Who was the authority competent to decide on the release of these people?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was ordered to protect them from the mujahedin and from others who might harm them, and we were subordinated to the command of the 306th. They could have appeared, or rather their security men could have appeared, or perhaps someone from an even higher level. Our duty was just to prevent the mujahedin, for example, from doing anything, or perhaps others. Perhaps there were people who had suffered at the hands of the Croats. And as a result, they might have wanted to do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... say that these decisions were left with the army, that the army had to take the position whether to release the person or not. I'm not sure exactly what you are implying.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. None of them asked to be released. And when it was time to exchange them, they were exchanged. That's all I can say. My duty was to provide security for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have very few questions for you. At the beginning you said that you were a policeman in Travnik. What do you do now? Do you have a rank? What do you do in the police.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm a sergeant in the police in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: You said a while ago that you were resubordinated to the 306th Brigade at a given point in time. When this was done, was it possible for you to forward reports to the civilian authorities in Travnik, or was it necessary for the 306th Brigade to forward such reports.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, we never forwarded our reports to the 306th, in spite of the fact that we were subordinated to them. We always sent our reports to Travnik, to the headquarters of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Does Defence have any questions, any additional questions for the witness? We have another five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have just three questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In answer to Justice Swart a while ago, you said your duty was to prevent the mujahedin from doing anything. Could you elaborate for me, how were you supposed to prevent them? What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: We were guarding the civilians who were inside, and it was our duty to protect them, not just from the mujahedin but from anyone who might want to do something to them. It was our duty to prevent anything being done to them to the extent that this was possible. I can remember one incident, only one incident. I think one mujahedin wanted to get in. I wasn't there, my colleagues were. The situation was a little tense. But they prevented him from entering. I think there was only one such mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in response to Judge Rasoazanany and I think Ms. Residovic, you spoke about the Vlasic incident and the fact that you were instructed to avoid conflicts. And you said that they settled accounts with them. They settled accounts with the mujahedins. Could you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what you mean when you say "they settled accounts." Who settled accounts? How were the accounts settled and why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. But my learned colleague has quoted the witness and said he said that someone settled accounts with the mujahedin. However, with regard to Mount Vlasic, I'd be grateful if my learned colleague could say when the witness made such a statement because I don't remember this being said before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Page 67, line 2 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is the question that you would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think my colleague probably didn't remember that you did indicate the bodies -- soldiers who had died, and as a result of that your instructions were that you were to try to avoid as much conflict as possible. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I answered that question. And I said that we were told not to engage in a conflict with them. We were told to deal with the situation in a calm way. I mentioned Vlasic. I mentioned the civilian police who were guarding the relay on Vlasic, and we had been captured. There were men who were killed. We didn't have enough trained policemen. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. And then you continued by saying "we settled accounts with them." And I believe you were referring to the mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't perhaps say that we settled accounts with them. I said that -- how should I put it? They didn't exactly respect the law, but during a certain period, I can't remember the year, many of them were arrested. They left the country. They were driven away, et cetera. But I don't know what I was speaking about, but that's something I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And this would be my last question to you: I think you still have it with you, Prosecution Exhibit 204. Number 7 under the order it, says "Individual movement by armed persons must be stopped and these persons disarmed and registered." Could you please elaborate for me or clarify if the mujahedins would have been considered as armed persons, would they have been considered as part of that group there? Would they have fallen in that category?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they should have fallen into that category. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, they should have fallen into that category. I agree with you. And were they disarmed? Was the order obeyed?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: As a rule, we would try to stop them. Our men would try to stop them, but they would refuse to stop. While they were passing by in their vehicles, they would just continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So the order was not carried out in full.

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that as far as they were concerned, we were told to avoid engaging in conflicts with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I have been following the procedure correctly, I think that the party calling the witness has the right to ask the last questions. I just have one question for the witness, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, with regard to the last question put to you by my learned colleague and in relation to item 7 in the document mentioned, could you tell us whether you registered and informed your superiors in the Travnik police and administration about the movement of these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that this was possible for us at the time, we did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you still give the same reasons that you have given to the Chamber? Would you still say why you didn't use force?

utterances.speaker: SEJAD JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes your testimony in the courtroom. Thank you for answering the questions put to you by all the parties and the Judges. I wish you a good trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning to the Defence. We have two witnesses scheduled for tomorrow. How will we be proceeding in order to complete the examination of these witnesses at 1.45 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so far, I had said that the examination of the witnesses would depend on the length of the cross-examination. But as you have noticed, my learned colleagues from the Prosecution used up more time than we did. And I think that I could answer this question if my colleagues from the Prosecution can also answer the same question. I would try to limit the examination-in-chief for both witnesses and reduce the length of the examination by half an hour. They were supposed to testify for an hour and a half, and I will do my best to ensure that their examination-in-chief doesn't last more than an hour. If we could hear what the Prosecution has to say, we might be able to see whether we could conclude with their testimony tomorrow. If it's not possible to conclude with these two witnesses tomorrow, then I would not try to reduce the length of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I am now addressing the Prosecution. You have heard what the Defence said. Defence counsel could examine each witness for one hour tomorrow. But in such a case, the Prosecution should proceed in the same manner. In total, that would amount to four hours. And as you know, we only have 3 hours and 45 minutes, effectively. And that's a problem already. If you all go to the crux of the matter, we might be able to finish with these witnesses tomorrow. Mr. Mundis, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution will certainly endeavour to not consume longer in cross-examining the witness than the direct examination. But as Your Honours are well aware, it's very difficult for us to predict how long it will take us to cross-examine the witness both because we have only a very limited amount of information as to what the witness will testify about prior to their testimony; that is, we have their very brief Rule 65 ter summaries in the annex B, number one. Number two, of course, the fact that the witness might take an hour on direct and an hour on cross, it's very difficult for us to predict how long the re-examination might be or questions from Your Honours. So it's all very, very difficult to predict. We certainly don't purposefully consume great periods of time in our cross-examination. We're doing the best we can with the information that we have prior to the testimony of the witnesses. The only other point I would simply ask at this point, Mr. President, in terms of planning: If the Chamber were of the view that we need to finish both witnesses tomorrow, we would be grateful for any indications that might put us in a situation where we're sitting later than we're planned to sit tomorrow, again, simply for planning purposes as we did last Thursday where we sat much longer than the schedule. We would appreciate it if the Chamber could give us any indications of whether or not that might be an option. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we're not able to finish with the second witness tomorrow by 1.45, it will be necessary to continue examining this witness on Monday. At the moment, what is the Defence's schedule for next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session. Now that we are in public session, I inform you that we are adjourning, and we shall recommence tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
